opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it started from a fairly simple intuition. If you look at what makes humans general, it's not that we're the best at any single task. A lot of animals see better, run faster, or have better memory for certain things. What makes us different is that we can use language to reason, to plan, and to learn new things very quickly from just a few examples or instructions. Language is kind of the most general tool humans have invented. It's how we think about things we've never seen before, and it's how we pass knowledge across people and generations.

So when I was in undergrad at Tsinghua, in the Yao Class, I was doing more theoretical stuff at first, and then I got into vision and other areas. But I always felt something was missing. A lot of AI back then was very task-specific. You train a model for Go, or for an Atari game, or for image classification, and it's superhuman there but can't transfer anywhere else. Language seemed like the place where generalization could actually happen, because language covers almost everything humans care about.

Then the question became: language is great, but a language model by itself just predicts text. How do you make it actually *do* things in the world? That's where agents come in. For me, an agent is a system that can interact with an environment, take actions, get feedback, and keep going toward some goal. If you combine the generality of language with the ability to act, you get something that can potentially solve open-ended problems, not just answer questions.

That's what led to work like ReAct, which is basically about letting the model interleave reasoning and acting: think a bit, take an action, look at the result, think again. And Tree of Thoughts was about letting the model explore different reasoning paths, more like deliberate thinking than just going left to right. The underlying belief is that reasoning itself can be treated as a kind of action. Thinking is an action that doesn't change the external world, but it changes your internal state, and that turns out to be incredibly powerful for generalization.

I also think there's a practical side. For a long time, people in reinforcement learning had very good algorithms but not very good priors, and people in NLP had very good priors but not much interaction with environments. Language agents are where those two finally meet. Once you have strong priors from pretraining, RL and interaction suddenly start to generalize, which they mostly didn't before.

So to me, language and agents aren't just one path among many. They're kind of the natural combination. Language gives you generality, and agency gives you the ability to turn that generality into real impact. And increasingly I think the interesting question isn't just "can we make models smarter on benchmarks," but "what are the right tasks and environments where this actually creates value for people." That's the part I find most exciting right now.

r001.rationale: The response says language “covers almost everything humans care about” and is a tool for thinking about things never seen, identifying its broad representational reach as a source of generality.

r002.rationale: It says combining language with an agent’s ability to act could solve open-ended problems, and describes language and agents as a natural combination for general AI.

r003.rationale: The response says much AI was task-specific, but does not attribute that specialization to the difficulty of the original ambition to build general agents.

r004.rationale: It does not connect advances after 2015 to a renewed pursuit of general systems or mention that period.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the attraction comes from two directions that eventually converged for me.

The first is language itself. When I started doing research, I was drawn to the idea that language is not just a way of transmitting information, it's a way of thinking. Humans think in language, plan in language, reflect on mistakes in language. So if you want to build something that can reason generally, language is a very natural substrate. It's compositional, it's open-ended, and crucially it's how humans have encoded almost all of our accumulated knowledge about the world. A model that masters language inherits a lot of priors about how the world works for free.

The second direction is agents. If you look at how intelligence has historically been studied, there's this long tradition in reinforcement learning of learning through interaction with an environment: acting, observing, getting feedback. That framing feels right to me, because intelligence isn't just knowing things, it's doing things, pursuing goals over time, dealing with consequences. But classical RL agents had a problem. They learned from scratch in very narrow environments, like Atari games, and nothing transferred.

What excited me, around the time of GPT-3 and after, was realizing that these two things could fix each other's weaknesses. Language models have enormous priors but no ability to act or ground themselves. RL agents can act but have no priors. If you put a language model in the loop as the agent, suddenly you have an agent that already knows a lot about the world, and it can use reasoning as a kind of internal action. That's really the idea behind work like ReAct: thinking and acting are not separate, the reasoning trace is itself a kind of action that helps you decide the next external action. And Reflexion extends that, where the agent learns from its own failures through verbal feedback rather than gradient updates.

I also think the environment question is underrated. People focus a lot on model architecture, but what really defines an agent is the task and the environment it's embedded in. That's why I spent time on things like WebShop and SWE-bench, because if you want agents that are generally useful, you need environments that actually look like the real world, with real tools, real messiness, real consequences. Digital environments are especially interesting because they're where a huge fraction of human work already happens, and they're cheap to scale.

So to put it simply: language gives you the priors and the reasoning medium, agents give you the grounding and the goal-directedness, and the combination feels to me like the most practical path toward something that's actually generally capable, not just generally knowledgeable.

r001.rationale: It describes language as compositional and open-ended, a natural substrate for general reasoning, and a way humans have encoded accumulated knowledge about the world.

r002.rationale: It presents agents as necessary for acting, grounding, and pursuing goals, and calls combining agents with language models a practical path toward general capability.

r003.rationale: It says classical RL agents learned in narrow environments, but does not attribute AI research’s increasing specialization to the difficulty of the original goal of building general agents.

r004.rationale: It mentions GPT-3 and later work, but does not connect AI advances after 2015 to a renewed pursuit of general systems.

astra-6.text:
What attracts me is that language is both a way to describe the world and a way to act in it. We use language to communicate, but also to break down problems, make plans, and reflect on mistakes. So it offers a very flexible interface for intelligence. You don’t necessarily need a separate formulation for every task—you can express many different tasks in the same medium.

But language alone isn’t the whole story. An agent has to connect its reasoning to something outside itself. It takes an action, gets feedback, and updates what it does next. That connection is exciting to me because a plausible answer and a successful action are different things. The world can tell you that your reasoning was wrong.

So I see language and agents as complementary. Language gives us a general way to represent and reason about problems; interaction gives that reasoning a purpose and a test. The question becomes: can a system use what it knows to accomplish something, discover what it doesn’t know, and improve through that process? That feels like a productive way to approach general intelligence.

r001.rationale: It describes language as a flexible medium for many tasks, but does not clearly say it can represent almost anything as the source of its generality.

r002.rationale: It presents agents and interaction as complementary to language and as a productive path toward general intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss AI research becoming more specialized or link that to the difficulty of building general agents.

r004.rationale: It does not mention advances after 2015 or a renewed pursuit of general systems.

sol-6.1.text:
What attracts me to language is that it’s both a way to represent knowledge and a way to do things. We use language to describe the world, but also to reason, make plans, ask for help, and coordinate with other people. So it provides a very natural connection between intelligence and action.

With agents, the interesting shift is from producing an answer to interacting with an environment. You take an action, get feedback, and revise your plan. A model might give a convincing explanation of how to solve a problem, but when it actually has to solve it, missing assumptions become visible. Can it find the information it needs? Can it recognize a mistake and recover?

To me, putting language and agents together offers a promising path toward more general intelligence: language gives you a flexible interface, and interaction grounds that flexibility in consequences. The exciting question is how far we can go from generating plausible text to reliably accomplishing useful tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says language represents knowledge and supports several kinds of reasoning and action, but does not say it can represent almost anything or identify that breadth as the source of its generality.

r002.rationale: It describes language and agents as a promising path toward more general intelligence, but does not express that achieving very general AI requires building an agent.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute AI research’s specialization to the difficulty of building general agents.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect post-2015 AI advances to renewed pursuit of general systems.
